newsitem.title: USA: Lehman settles with SEC on supervisory case.
newsitem.headline: Lehman settles with SEC on supervisory case.

text.p: Lehman Bros Inc agreed Thursday to be censured and pay a civil penalty of $50,000 to settle allegations it failed to properly supervise a broker who overcharged two customers more than $1 million in the purchase of government securities, regulators said.
The Securities and Exchange Commission said Lehman agreed to the settlement without admitting or denying guilt.

The broker in question, Stanley Feminella, 48, handled the accounts of the customers -- Consumer Union of the United States Inc and its employee pension fund -- from 1984 to February 1991 in three brokerages.
The period included his employment with Shearson Lehman Bros. Inc., the predecessor company of Lehman Bros, that began in late 1988, when the brokerage was involved in securities retailing.

Most of Shearson's retail offices were sold to Smith Barney, Harris Upham & Co in 1993. Lehman Bros, a unit of Lehman Bros Holdings Inc, is answerable for any regulatory liability by Shearson prior to the sale of its retail operations, the SEC contended.
Shearson terminated Feminella in 1991, the SEC said.

The SEC said that while at Shearson, Consumers Union bought through Feminella $38.5 million in government securities. Shearson allowed Feminella to charge a three-point sales credit, which when added to the spreads charged by the firm, resulted in the customers paying undisclosed, excessive markups, the SEC said.
The markups ranged from 3.5 percent to 4.7 percent and the customers paid at least $1.39 million in markups, of which Feminella received at least $904,000, the SEC sasid.
The SEC said the securities were purchased "at prices that bore no reasonable relationship" to prevailing market prices.

The SEC said it found that Shearson lacked sufficient, firm-wide policies and procedures designed to prevent and detect excessive markups, particularly on large retail transactions the firm did with Consumers Union and the pension fund.
It also found that violated books and record keeping rules by failing to to keep confirmation records about Consumer Union's purchases.
In January, Feminella, 48, was charged by the SEC in a separate civil complaint, accusing him of paying kickbacks to a former financial officer of Consumers Union in return for the group's business.
The Consumers Union official, David Granston, has settled that case; litigation continues against Feminella, the SEC said.
